content: Chagas disease, also referred to as American trypanosomiasis, is an illness caused by a parasitic organism. The parasite is transmitted to humans primarily through the feces of triatomine bugs, commonly known as kissing bugs. These bugs often defecate while biting a person. Infection typically occurs when an individual inadvertently rubs the bug's feces into the bite wound while scratching or when the feces come into contact with the eyes or mouth. Some individuals may experience localized swelling around the bite site. However, the majority of infected individuals remain asymptomatic throughout their lives, even though the parasite persists in their bodies. Approximately one-third of those infected will develop severe complications later in life, such as cardiac disorders or gastrointestinal issues. These complications can arise regardless of whether the person exhibited early symptoms of the disease. Chagas disease is primarily found in rural areas of Mexico, Central America, and South America, where triatomine bugs are prevalent. Travelers to these regions are generally at low risk of contracting the disease. However, individuals who sleep outdoors or stay in poorly constructed housing, such as thatch, mud, or adobe structures, are at a higher risk of being bitten by triatomine bugs. There is currently no vaccine or medication available to prevent Chagas disease. Travelers can reduce their risk of infection by taking the following precautions: 1. Avoid Bug Bites: Stay and sleep in rooms that are screened or air-conditioned. Avoid sleeping in thatch, mud, or adobe housing in areas where triatomine bugs are common. Use insecticides in and around such homes. Use insecticide-treated bed nets for additional protection. Cover exposed skin by wearing long-sleeved shirts, long pants, and hats. Apply EPA-registered insect repellents containing active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanone. Always follow the product instructions and reapply as directed. If using sunscreen, apply sunscreen first and insect repellent second. 2. Special Considerations for Children: Do not use products containing OLE or PMD on children under three years of age. Avoid applying insect repellent to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, cuts, or irritated skin. Adults should spray insect repellent onto their hands first and then apply it to a child’s face. 3. Protective Clothing and Gear: Wear clothing and use gear (such as boots, pants, socks, and tents) treated with permethrin. Pre-treated items remain protective after multiple washes; check the product information for details on the duration of protection. If treating clothing and gear yourself, carefully follow the product instructions. Do not apply permethrin directly to the skin. By adhering to these preventive measures, travelers can significantly reduce their risk of exposure to Chagas disease.
